review_comments.body: Bug in the matcher logic: the substring bounds and the return condition are both wrong. The context prefix is 6 chars (sessionType[0-2], tokenType[2-4], grantType[4-6]), so the grant shortcut is at index 4-6, not 3-5. Also the condition is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(...).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false when the grant DOES match, which is the opposite of the intended behavior. Should be `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.

Copy-paste bug in the null check: the second `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` checks `grantType` again instead of `rawTokenId`. This means a null rawTokenId will not be caught. Should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

grantsByShortcuts and grantsToShortcuts are populated in postInit but there is no dedicated collision detection for OAuth2 grant shortcuts themselves before UNKNOWN is inserted. If two grants share the same shortcut, grantsByShortcuts would silently overwrite while grantsToShortcuts would have two entries, and the size mismatch check would catch it - however this ordering means the error message may be misleading. Minor: consider validating shortcuts are exactly 2 chars, since encodeTokenId assumes a fixed 6-char prefix; a grant returning a shortcut of other length would produce malformed token IDs that fail decoding.

getClientSession().getUserSession() may return null in some transient/edge flows, leading to a NullPointerException when calling getPersistenceState(). Consider a null check to fall back to UNKNOWN sessionType.

review_comments.body: canManage() (all-groups) checks for VIEW or MANAGE scopes, which is inconsistent with canManage(group) that only checks MANAGE. A caller with only VIEW-all-groups permission would pass canManage(). This likely should check only MANAGE (and possibly VIEW for consistency, but VIEW granting manage is a privilege escalation).

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses resourceStore.findByType to enumerate group resources and checks VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS per resource. However, this only returns groups that have an explicit resource; it does not account for an 'all-groups' permission granting view-members. Callers relying on this set (e.g. user search filtering) may miss users when only an all-groups permission exists.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission now only short-circuits on root.users().canView() and no longer on canManage(). Previously getGroupsWithViewPermission checked both canView() and canManage(). A user with only MANAGE_USERS (manage but not view) would no longer get the empty-set short-circuit and would proceed to per-group evaluation. Verify MANAGE_USERS implies canView() so this is intentional.

Removing the public static searchGroupModelsByAttributes method is a breaking API change in server-spi-private. If any external/downstream code depends on it, this will break compilation. Consider deprecating rather than removing.

The .filter(usersEvaluator::canView) was removed from searchForUser. Filtering now relies solely on the GROUPS session attribute set from getGroupIdsWithViewPermission. This changes behavior: previously each returned user was re-checked via canView. Removing the filter may expose users the caller cannot view (e.g., service accounts or users matched by criteria but outside permitted groups). Confirm the store-level filtering fully replaces canView filtering.

Same concern as UsersResource: previous behavior wrapped the group-permission lookup in an `if (!auth.users().canView())` guard. Now getGroupIdsWithViewPermission is always called and the attribute set unconditionally. Ensure getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty set when the caller can view all users (it does short-circuit on canView), otherwise the GROUPS attribute would wrongly restrict results for privileged admins.

When resource is null and falls back to the resource-type resource, permissions are evaluated with resource.getScopes() (all scopes of the type). This means an all-groups permission granting any single scope could satisfy checks for scopes it wasn't granted, because getScopes() returns the resource's full scope set rather than the granted scopes. Verify evaluatePermission actually restricts to granted scopes; if it evaluates all type scopes, this could over-grant.

review_comments.body: `get_queue_for_group` uses Python's built-in `hash()` for group assignment. `hash()` for strings is randomized per-process (PYTHONHASHSEED), which is fine within a single process, but note that `hash()` can return negative values — `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` works correctly in Python since `%` on a negative gives a non-negative result, so this is OK. However, relying on `hash()` means a group's queue assignment is not stable across process restarts; if ordering guarantees are expected across rebalances this could be a concern. Consider using a stable hash (e.g. md5/xxhash) for determinism.

OffsetTracker relies on per-partition locks, but `_get_partition_lock` itself is not thread-safe: `self.partition_locks.setdefault` is called after a non-atomic `.get()`. `setdefault` on a dict is effectively atomic under CPython's GIL, so it works, but this pattern is fragile. More importantly, `add_offset` may be called concurrently from `submit` (main thread) while `get_committable_offsets` iterates — this is guarded by the lock, but the initial lock creation race for a new partition could allow two threads to briefly use different lock objects. Consider creating partition locks upfront on partition assignment.

`submit()` catches exceptions from the decoder and marks the offset complete, but a subtle issue: if `self.queue_pool.submit()` succeeds in adding the offset but then an unrelated later line raised, the except block would call `add_offset`/`complete_offset` again — however since submit already added and enqueued, the double add_offset is idempotent (set) but complete_offset would prematurely mark an in-flight offset complete, potentially committing before the worker processes it. The try block should be narrowed to only wrap decoding so a successful submit is not followed by the fallback completion path.

`submit()` on the underlying `queue.Queue` uses `put()` with no maxsize, so the docstring claim of 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' is not accurate — the queues are unbounded and will never block/apply backpressure. Consider setting a `maxsize` on the queues to actually get backpressure, or update the docstring.

In `get_committable_offsets`, iterating `range(start, max_offset + 1)` can be very expensive if offsets are sparse/large (e.g. after a gap the range spans many values). Since Kafka offsets are monotonic this is usually contiguous, but a large gap between last_committed and max would cause a large loop each commit cycle (every 1s). Consider iterating over sorted present offsets instead of a numeric range.

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` catches `queue.ShutDown` from `work_queue.get()` to break, but the inner try also catches `queue.ShutDown` — the outer `except queue.ShutDown` on get() is correct. However, when shutdown is requested via `self.shutdown = True` but the worker is blocked on `work_queue.get()` (which blocks indefinitely with no timeout), it will not wake up until `queue.shutdown()` is called. The `shutdown` boolean flag is effectively redundant given the blocking get; relying solely on it without queue.shutdown() would hang. This works only because shutdown() calls q.shutdown(), but the flag check at top of loop is racy/ineffective.

`shutdown()` sets `self.queue_pool = None` after shutting it down. But `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` asserts `self.queue_pool is not None` and the SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy holds its own reference to the pool. If create_with_partitions is called again after shutdown (e.g. on rebalance), queue_pool would be None and the assert fails, since it's only constructed once in __init__. Consider re-creating the pool or not nulling it out.

review_comments.body: The `optimized_pagination` query param combined with superuser/global-access gating exposes the `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True`, which permits negative cursor offsets. This appears to be an access-control/data-exposure risk: negative offsets bypass the normal `max(0, offset)` clamping and allow traversal 'beyond normal pagination bounds'. The comment even states data is accessed 'beyond normal pagination bounds', which is suspicious for an audit-log endpoint.

Changing the base paginator to allow negative offsets when `cursor.is_prev` alters behavior for ALL existing paginators, not just the new optimized one. Previously `stop = offset + limit + extra` used the raw offset; now for non-prev cursors it clamps to `max(0, offset)` but for prev cursors it allows negative offsets. Negative Django slice indices (`queryset[-5:...]`) count from the end of the queryset, returning unintended rows rather than an empty/clamped result. This is a correctness and potential data-leak bug.

Negative offset slicing via Django ORM does NOT 'handle boundary conditions' safely as the comment claims. `queryset[negative_offset:stop]` triggers negative indexing which Django resolves relative to the end of the result set, exposing rows the caller should not reach. The security assumption that 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' is unfounded — the queryset is the same audit-log queryset and offset manipulation lets a user page into arbitrary positions.

Reducing the redirect-chain loop bound from 10000 to 1000 changes correctness guarantees: segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects will no longer be joined correctly. This is an unexplained functional regression unrelated to the eviction feature; the original comment warned about depth limits and lowering it 10x narrows the safe range.

`zunionstore` return value is used for `span_count`, but when both the span_key and parent_key branches execute, the second assignment overwrites the first rather than reflecting the final set cardinality after both unions. The subsequent `if span_count == 0` fallback to `zcard` only triggers when neither branch ran, so in the single-branch case span_count reflects that union's total which is correct, but relying on zunionstore's returned count across two operations is fragile. Consider always using `zcard(set_key)` after unions to get the true size before eviction.

Removing the `max_segment_spans` guard eliminates protection against unbounded segment span counts. Previously segments exceeding `max_segment_spans` were skipped with a metric/log; now only byte-size is checked. Although the Lua script caps at 1000 via zpopmin, the loader-side safety check is silently dropped, which reduces defense-in-depth and removes the `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric.

`val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct key access and will raise KeyError if the field is absent from an incoming span event, unlike the surrounding `.get()` usage for optional fields. If `end_timestamp_precise` is not guaranteed present in all producers/schema versions, this can crash the consumer. Confirm the schema mandates this field or use `.get()` with a sensible default.

review_comments.body: The caching logic is broken: the cache stores only the allowlist eligibility (`is_eligible`), but the cache key does not include the dataset/query context. However `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` is applied on both cache hit and miss, so that's fine. The real issue is that `cache.get` returning `None` is used as the cache-miss sentinel, but a cached value of `False` is a valid result — `if cached_result is not None` handles this correctly. However, caching allowlist eligibility for 60s introduces a race with `invalidate_upsampling_cache`, and more importantly the cache key uses Python's `hash()` on a tuple which is not stable across processes when `PYTHONHASHSEED` randomization is enabled for tuples of ints—actually ints hash deterministically, but relying on `hash()` for cache keys is fragile. Consider building the key from the raw sorted project ids instead of `hash()`.

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` compares `project_id in allowlist`, but the allowlist option values may be strings or the project_ids may differ in type. Ensure type consistency (e.g., cast both to int) to avoid silent membership failures.

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` is called on `query_columns` and reassigned to `final_columns`, but for the RPC top_events path and non-RPC top_events path both are guarded by the same outer `if upsampling_enabled` set once before `if top_events > 0`. This is fine, but note the RPC and standard non-top-events branches re-run the transform on `query_columns` (not `final_columns`), which is redundant but harmless. However, upsampling via `sum(sample_weight)` on the RPC dataset (spans/EAP) will fail since `upsampled_count` is only defined in the discover/errors SnQL dataset, not for RPC. If `use_rpc` is true and upsampling is enabled, the transformed `upsampled_count() as count` column will not resolve. Guard upsampling to non-RPC paths or ensure RPC supports it.

The bare `except Exception: pass` blocks silently swallow all errors when reading/parsing the client_sample_rate. This can hide real bugs. Prefer catching specific exceptions (e.g., TypeError, ValueError, AttributeError) and avoid a blanket except.

`upsampled_count` uses `sum(sample_weight)` but has `default_result_type="number"`, while the standard `count()` returns integer. The result is wrapped in `toInt64`, so the effective type is integer. Consider `default_result_type="integer"` for consistency with `count()` and correct client formatting.

The caching path in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is never tested. Since caching introduces significant behavioral complexity (60s TTL, invalidation), add tests covering cache hit/miss and invalidation to prevent regressions.

The docstring claims allowlist eligibility is cached for consistency, but caching per (org, projects) while the allowlist is a global option means a global allowlist change won't invalidate all cached org/project combinations. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` requires knowing the exact project_ids set, which is impractical when the option changes globally. This can lead to stale eligibility for up to 60s across many keys with no way to invalidate them all.

review_comments.body: The permission denial cache introduces a correctness risk: when a permission is granted after a prior denial was cached, the denial cache entry (TTL = shortCacheTTL) will continue to return Allowed=false until it expires, even though the regular permCache may have been updated. Because the denial cache is checked first and short-circuits before consulting the permCache, a newly-granted permission won't take effect until the denial entry expires. Consider invalidating the denial cache when permissions change, or ensure both caches share consistent invalidation semantics.

On a cache hit where checkPermission returns allowed=false, the code falls through to getIdentityPermissions and re-evaluates. This means a cached deny (allowed=false) does not short-circuit here, which is inconsistent with the permDenialCache logic and causes an unnecessary DB fetch on every negative cached permission. This may partly defeat the caching optimization for denials that aren't yet in the denial cache.

The denial is cached unconditionally for all identity types and requests, including for TypeRenderService/anonymous where getCachedIdentityPermissions always returns ErrNotFound. More importantly, caching a denial without also keying on any versioning/invalidation means stale denies persist. Also, the Set error is ignored — consider logging it consistently with other cache operations.

userPermDenialCacheKey includes name and parent but the underlying permission grant (permCache) is keyed only by namespace/user/action. A denial cached for (name, parent) will not be invalidated when the user's permissions for that action change, leading to stale denies. review_comments.body: The computed property keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are invalid. `z.string().toString()` returns a generic string like `"ZodString"`, so both computed keys resolve to string literals (and the second overwrites nothing meaningful). This does not create a schema that accepts arbitrary numeric/unknown properties as intended. Use `.passthrough()` or `.catchall(z.unknown())` on the object schema instead.

`minimumTokenResponseSchema` does not define a `refresh_token` property (and does not passthrough), so accessing `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token` when the minimum schema is used will always be undefined, forcing the fallback `"refresh_token"` string. This could write a bogus refresh token into the credential.
`response.statusText !== "OK"` is an unreliable check. With fetch, `statusText` is often empty (e.g. HTTP/2) or varies by server. Use `!response.ok` or check `response.status` instead.

`salesforceTokenSchema` requires `refresh_token` to be absent but the parsed response is spread with `refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token`. However the schema itself doesn't validate `refresh_token`; more importantly this refresh runs unconditionally on every service construction, adding a network call and DB write even when the token isn't expired. Consider only refreshing when expired.

The credential-sync fetch does not check `response.ok` nor set a Content-Type header. Downstream callers (e.g. handleErrorsJson) may partially handle this, but silently returning a non-OK response as if it were a valid token response can lead to confusing failures. Also the return type differs between branches (raw fetch Response vs. refreshFunction result), which callers like zoho-bigin/zohocrm treat as an axios response (`tokenInfo.data`)—those will break when the sync branch returns a fetch Response.
Webhook secret comparison uses a non-constant-time `!==` string comparison, which is vulnerable to timing attacks. Consider using crypto.timingSafeEqual for secret verification.

`symmetricDecrypt` and `JSON.parse` are not wrapped in try/catch. Malformed `keys` or a wrong encryption key will throw an unhandled error resulting in a 500 with a stack trace rather than a controlled 400 response.

`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is typed as `string | undefined` (result of `&&` between two strings) rather than a boolean. Consuming code treats it as boolean; wrap with `!!(...)` or `Boolean(...)` for a proper boolean and clearer typing.

review_comments.body: The try/catch wraps a forEach over async delete functions (deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async and not awaited). Errors thrown inside the async reminder functions will not be caught by this try/catch since the promises are not awaited. Consider using Promise.all with await, or these errors will go unhandled.

If client.request fails for one reminder inside the for-loop, the entire catch block is hit and remaining reminders are skipped, and the successfully-cancelled reminders may not be deleted (since Promise.all is only reached after the loop completes). Consider per-reminder try/catch so a single SendGrid failure doesn't prevent processing/cleaning up the rest.

The new 'cancelled' column is nullable Boolean (Boolean?) with no default. The scheduleEmailReminders query filters on `cancelled: true`, which works, but consider giving it a default of false (@default(false)) for clearer semantics and to avoid three-state boolean logic (null/true/false).

When immediateDelete is true, the SendGrid cancel request is issued but the WorkflowReminder row is never deleted from the DB. Previously the reminder was cleaned up (via deleteMany in callers that were removed). This may leave orphaned reminder records for immediate-delete paths (deleted workflow, deleted steps).

Prisma and PrismaPromise are imported as values now (removed 'import type'), but they are only used as types. This can cause unnecessary runtime imports; keep 'import type' for type-only imports to satisfy isolatedModules/verbatimModuleSyntax.
